2021_193_9_d_hamby_paper_2006.paragraph: "Radiofrequency and Public Health" is a four-page white paper by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., dated November 2006 and carried as item 9.D. in the June 15, 2021 Troy Board of Education packet. Hamby, a professor of health physics at Oregon State University and a former University of Michigan School of Public Health professor, measures typical PCS and cellular tower output against federal exposure guidelines. Its central figure is that the maximum power density 100 feet laterally from a cell antenna element calculates to 0.010 mw/cm2, or 100 times below the NCRP limit of 1 mw/cm2, and it concludes that health risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are negligible.
2021_193_9_d_hamby_paper_2006.page:
**Document and author**
White paper titled "Radiofrequency and Public Health / The Impact of Radiofrequency Transmissions on Public Health," by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., November 2006; four numbered pages. Hamby is Professor of Health Physics (radiation protection) at Oregon State University, a former professor in the University of Michigan's School of Public Health and a graduate of the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health, with 20 years in environmental and occupational health protection including 6 years as a research scientist with Westinghouse. He serves on Scientific Committee #64-23 of the NCRP and Committee N13.60 of ANSI, sits on the editorial boards of Health Physics and Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, and has served as a technical expert for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

**Scope and units**
Public concern that began with extremely low frequency fields near electric-power lines has extended to radiofrequency transmissions used in wireless communications; the paper surveys typical exposure levels and federal guidelines in the PCS and cellular range. Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz), one repetition per second; a heart beating 70 times per second beats at 70 Hz, and a 1 GHz chip performs 1 billion operations per second. PCS operates in the 1.9 GHz range. Power is measured in Watts; a 100 W bulb uses twice the energy of a 50 W bulb, and PCS towers output about 200 Watts in each of three sectors. Exposure limits are expressed as power density in mw/cm2, where 1000 milliwatts equals 1 Watt.

**Exposure limits**

| Body / jurisdiction | Public limit |
| --- | --- |
| FCC (standardization suggested August 1, 1996, adopting NCRP recommendation) | 1 mw/cm2 |
| Australia and New Zealand | identical to NCRP |
| Netherlands | twice that value |
| ICNIRP (2 GHz and higher) | 1 mw/cm2 |

Limits are set into law by the FCC on recommendation from the IEEE, ANSI and NCRP. For perspective, the metabolic heat production rate of an average human at rest is about 5 mw/cm2, rising with activity to as much as 80 mw/cm2 depending on age, gender, size and physical fitness.

**Calculated tower emissions**

| Distance from antenna | Maximum power density | Relation to standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 100 feet | 0.010 mw/cm2 | 100 times lower |
| 200 feet | 0.0025 mw/cm2 | 400 times lower |
| 400 feet | 0.00063 mw/cm2 | 1,600 times lower |

Power density equals total power divided by the area through which it is directed; for a typical cell tower that area is 4πr2/6, the surface of a spherical triangle of radius r with a horizontal angle of 120 degrees and a vertical angle of approximately 90 degrees. The worked example uses a transmitter output of 200 Watts (200,000 milliwatts) and a distance of 100 feet (3,048 centimeters). Because the inverse-square principle applies, doubling the distance reduces power density four times. Actual ground-level values are lower still because most transmitted power is aimed at the horizon.

**Comparison with other RF sources**
A table lists anti-theft devices, automatic door openers, hand-held cellular, cordless phones, CB radio, mobile radio, PCS, microwave ovens, satellite communications, AM radio, FM radio, LORAN transmitters and television by frequency range (MHz) and maximum power (Watts). Television and radio towers are generally much taller and emit up to 5 million Watts; a 1,000 foot TV tower radiating 5 million Watts in all directions would have a power density at its base of 0.43 mw/cm2, more than 40% of the federal limit at that frequency. Baby monitors operate at a few Watts, so the power density 100 feet from a 200 Watt PCS transmitter equals that about four feet from a baby monitor.

**Conclusion**
Calculated and measured PCS power densities are many times lower than the 1 mw/cm2 standard. Most recent studies find no statistical difference between exposed and non-exposed persons; the minority reporting associations generally cannot establish causation, and rat studies frequently fail to replicate, one group's own triplicate experiment yielding one positive and two negative findings. Scientific studies have failed to demonstrate a human health effect from low-level radiofrequency fields, and risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are called negligible.
2021_193_9_d_hamby_paper_2006.verbose:
"RADIOFREQUENCY AND PUBLIC HEALTH: The Impact of Radiofrequency Transmissions on Public Health" is a four-page white paper written by David M. Hamby, Ph.D., dated November 2006, distributed as agenda item 9.D. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 15, 2021.

**Author credentials.** Dr. Hamby is described as currently Professor of Health Physics (radiation protection) at Oregon State University and a former professor in the University of Michigan's School of Public Health. He is a graduate of the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health and has spent 20 years studying environmental and occupational health protection, including 6 years working as a research scientist with Westinghouse. He serves on Scientific Committee #64-23 of the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP) and on Committee N13.60 of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). He sits on the Editorial Board for the Health Physics journal and for the journal of Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, and has served as a technical expert for the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

**Framing of the issue.** Over the past several years, the paper states, potential health impacts from exposure to electromagnetic fields have gained widespread public interest. Questions arose originally with regard to extremely low frequency electric and magnetic fields such as those found near electric-power lines. With the continued advancement of personal communications technology, similar concerns have arisen about electromagnetic transmissions in the radiofrequency region, including that used in wireless communications. The paper provides an overview of typical exposure levels and current federal exposure guidelines for radiofrequency electromagnetic waves in the frequency range utilized by PCS and cellular systems.

**Frequency and power.** Biological effects associated with exposure to intense electromagnetic fields, generally the result of thermal heating, depend on two characteristics of electromagnetic waves: frequency and power. Using speech as an analogy, frequency corresponds to pitch (treble or bass) and power to loudness. The scientific unit of frequency is the Hertz (Hz), representing one repetition per second; a heart beating 70 times per second would beat at a frequency of 70 Hz, and a computer chip operating at 1 GHz (gigahertz, giga meaning billion) performs 1 billion operations per second. A figure in the paper, an electromagnetic spectrum chart labeled with frequency in MHz and wavelength in meters, shows common uses across the spectrum — AM, FM, TV, mobile radio, CB radio, cordless phones, PCS, microwaves, infrared, visible light and x-rays — with a boundary marked between non-ionizing and ionizing radiation. PCS operates in the 1.9 GHz frequency range.

Power is measured in Watts (W), the amount of energy transferred during one second; a 100 W light bulb uses twice the energy of a 50 W light bulb. PCS towers operate at a typical power output in each of three sectors of about 200 Watts.

**Regulatory limits.** Radiofrequency exposure limits for members of the general public are set into law by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) based on recommendations from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements (NCRP). Today's standards identify the amount of energy per second, usually in milliwatts (1000 milliwatts equals 1 Watt), that can be transmitted through a square inch or, more typically, a square centimeter. Limits are therefore expressed as "power density" in mw/cm2 (milliwatts per square centimeter). On August 1, 1996 the FCC suggested standardization of exposure limits and adopted the NCRP recommendation of 1 mw/cm2. Regulations enacted within the previous couple of years in Australia and New Zealand stipulate identical limits to those of the NCRP, and regulations in the Netherlands allow exposure limits twice this value. The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) has also adopted an exposure limit of 1 mw/cm2 for members of the general public at frequencies of 2 GHz and higher.

**Metabolic comparison.** These limits are placed in perspective by comparison with the metabolic heat production rate for an average human at rest, about 5 mw/cm2. With increased activity, the metabolic heat production rate can naturally rise to as much as 80 mw/cm2, depending on physiological parameters such as age, gender, size and general physical fitness. The paper states that the heat production rate in the body caused by metabolism is thousands of times greater than any heat generated as a result of these transmissions.

**Calculated tower exposure.** PCS and cellular systems emit electromagnetic waves at frequencies in the GHz range with a nominal power of about 200 Watts per sector. Under these conditions the maximum power density at 100 feet laterally from the antenna element is calculated to be 0.010 mw/cm2, or 100 times below the NCRP limit. That estimate assumes transmission power is emitted equally in all directions within the focused area. In practice the bulk of transmitted power is aimed only at the horizon, so actual power levels on the ground 100 feet from the base of the tower are much less than the calculated value. Such power densities are far below the federal limit and a great deal lower than levels at which any type of biological effect has been observed.

**Comparison with other RF sources.** To illustrate what these power densities mean, the paper compares PCS transmissions with power density levels of other well-known radiofrequency devices, including baby monitors, anti-theft monitors and automatic door openers at department stores, cordless telephones, police/fire two-way radios, and television and radio broadcasting stations. Standard television and radio towers are generally much taller than PCS or cellular towers and emit signals with power levels up to 5 million Watts. A 1,000 foot TV tower holding an antenna that emits 5 million Watts in all directions potentially has a power density at its base of 0.43 mw/cm2, more than 40% of the federal limit for emissions at that frequency. Baby monitor transmitters operate at a power of a few Watts; therefore the power density at a distance of 100 feet from a 200 Watt PCS transmitter would equal the power density at about four (4) feet from a baby monitor. An accompanying table, "Some common radiofrequency sources," lists by frequency range (MHz) and maximum power (Watts) the following sources: anti-theft device, automatic door opener, hand-held cellular, cordless phone, CB radio, mobile radio, PCS, microwave oven, satellite communications, AM radio, FM radio, LORAN transmitter and television.

**Review of the literature.** The paper summarizes that calculated and measured power densities resulting from PCS transmissions are many times lower than the national and international RF standard of 1 mw/cm2. The most recent literature on potential health effects of RF exposure continues to show that a vast majority of studies find no statistical difference between exposed and non-exposed persons for the various biological effects studied. A few investigators suggest their data show associations between exposure and biological effect, but these studies are generally unable to establish a causal relationship. Repeated studies of effects on rats are many times unable to reproduce results; one group of investigators conducting their experiment in triplicate showed one positive and two negative findings for a particular biological effect in rats following exposure to radiofrequency radiation, a result the paper cites as demonstrating the variability of such research. Scientific studies have failed to demonstrate a human health effect from exposure to low-level radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, and the scientific data indicate that health risks from PCS or cellular RF transmissions are negligible.

**Calculation of maximum power density.** Power density can be calculated at any distance from an electromagnetic source if the source is assumed to emit from a single point: the total power emitted divided by the area through which the power is directed. For a typical cell tower that area is 4πr2/6, the surface area of a spherical triangle with radius r, a horizontal angle of 120 degrees and a vertical angle of approximately 90 degrees. The worked example assumes a transmitter power output of 200 Watts (200,000 milliwatts) and the shortest distance associated with an urban tower, 100 feet (3,048 centimeters). Because the inverse-square principle applies to electromagnetic emission sources, every doubling of distance reduces power density four times: at 100 feet horizontally from the top of a cell tower the maximum power density is 0.010 mw/cm2 (100 times lower than the RF standard); at 200 feet it would be four times lower, about 0.0025 mw/cm2 (400 times lower than the standard); and at 400 feet it is reduced to 0.00063 mw/cm2 (1,600 times lower than the standard). Power density therefore drops very rapidly with increasing distance from the emission source.

2021_194_9_d_rf_radiation_article_from_a.paragraph: "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval" is a site-leasing feature from the May 2009 issue of AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine, included as item 9.D. in the June 15, 2021 Troy Board of Education packet. It recounts a January 5 vote by the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education to keep in place an agreement with U.S. Cellular for a tower resembling a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. RF consultant Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions persuaded a majority of board members by showing that a nearby cell site lowers handset transmit power, reducing student exposure from 1,000 times (peak) below the FCC safety limit to 1 million times below it.
2021_194_9_d_rf_radiation_article_from_a.page:
**Publication**
Site-leasing article, "RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval," AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine, May 2009, pages 16, 18 and 19, www.agl-mag.com.

**The decision**
Members of the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted in the majority to keep in place a previously approved agreement with U.S. Cellular for a proposed cell tower that would take the place of, yet resemble, a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. The vote was taken on January 5 and followed concerns brought to the board by residents near the school about possible health effects of radio-frequency emanations from the tower. Although the Telecommunications Act of 1996 does not allow government agencies to take health effects of RF emitted from cell towers and other radio transmitters into account when making site-approval decisions, landlords may consider health effects when deciding whether to lease.

**The presenter**
U.S. Cellular asked Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions, Chandler, Ariz., to speak to board members about possible health effects. Wessel later described his presentation to AGL.

**The BioInitiative Report**
Local activists promoted a website against the proposed site, and one or more board members and residents referenced the "BioInitiative Report: A Rationale for a Biologically-based Public Exposure Standard for Electromagnetic Fields (ELF and RF)," published at www.bioinitiative.org. Wessel said the report claims a diverse range of adverse health effects related to RF emissions while dismissing the Nationwide Cohort Study in Denmark by Christoffer Johansen, John D. Boice Jr., Joseph K. McLaughlin and Jorgen H. Olsen, which included 420,095 cell phone users and found no significant link between cell phone use and cancer. The report suggests reducing RF exposure limits without specifying values, other than that "a precautionary limit of 0.1 µW/cm2 (which is also 0.614 volts per meter) should be adopted for outdoor, cumulative RF exposure." Wessel noted that any properly designed cellular or PCS site, with antennas at least 10 meters above ground level, already contributes less than that proposed precautionary limit in surrounding areas, while commercial TV and FM broadcast levels typically exceed it in every major metropolitan location in the country.

**Measurement method**
Wessel presented quantitative RF measurements taken with a selective radiation meter — a spectrum analyzer plus an isotropic antenna, the Narda SRM-3000 — one of a few portable spectrum analyzers designed and calibrated specifically for RF compliance safety measurements. It has a dynamic range much greater than broadband equipment and can discriminate measurements by frequency from 50 to 3000 MHz, isolating each license holder's contribution to the overall RF environment. With narrowband selectivity, power density levels can be measured down to the picowatt per square centimeter level.

**The handset argument**

| Condition | RF exposure to students |
| --- | --- |
| Serving cell site a mile or two away | handsets at full power; peak level 1,000 times below FCC limit |
| Cell site nearby | handsets at significantly lower power; level 1 million times below the safety limit |

At the Marshalltown school, service came from sites a mile or two away, and Wessel's measurements indicated handsets were powered up to full power during a call because the distant cell site controls handset power based on the received uplink signal. He told the board a quarter-watt handset next to the head delivers significantly more energy to the user than a 100-watt cell site 100 feet away and 100 feet above the ground, because of the inverse-square law, under which RF energy at a distance from a source drops by the square of the distance.

**Other points**
Wessel described measurements in a New York City neighborhood where FM and TV broadcast signals contributed a greater percentage of overall RF energy than a cell site across the street, with the total still well below the safety limit. He said objections are sometimes based on hysteria, that a worker on a tower may come close enough to an antenna — especially FM or TV broadcast antennas — to require an RF suit, and that a person would have to scale a cactus-disguised tower to its hidden antennas to receive unsafe exposure. A majority of the board members were persuaded, though "some people are never satisfied."
2021_194_9_d_rf_radiation_article_from_a.verbose:
"RF Measurements Help to Win Lease Approval" is a site-leasing feature published in the May 2009 issue of AGL (Above Ground Level) magazine (pages 16, 18 and 19; www.agl-mag.com), reproduced as agenda item 9.D. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of June 15, 2021. Its subhead states that showing how placing a cell site near a high school would reduce RF emissions from wireless handsets used by students helped persuade a board of education to leave in effect a previously approved lease for a tower at an athletic field.

**The Marshalltown decision.** Members of the Marshalltown (Iowa) Community School District Board of Education voted in the majority to keep in place an agreement with U.S. Cellular for a proposed cell tower that would take the place of, yet resemble, a light pole at the Marshalltown High School football field. The vote was taken on January 5. It came about as a result of concerns brought to the board by residents near the school regarding the possible effect upon health that radio-frequency emanations from the tower might have. The article notes that although the Telecommunications Act of 1996 does not allow government agencies to take into account the health effects of RF emitted from cell towers and other radio transmitters when making decisions about site approval, landlords may consider health effects when deciding whether to lease. A photo caption observes that cell towers near schools sometimes raise questions about possible health risks.

**The consultant.** U.S. Cellular asked Marv Wessel of Global RF Solutions, Chandler, Ariz., to speak to the board members about possible health effects. Afterward, AGL asked Wessel about his presentation, and the article is built around his account.

**Opposition and the BioInitiative Report.** Wessel said that in addition to local activists promoting a website against the proposed site, one or more board members and residents made reference to the "BioInitiative Report: A Rationale for a Biologically-based Public Exposure Standard for Electromagnetic Fields (ELF and RF)," published on the web at www.bioinitiative.org. "The report claims there is a diverse range of adverse health effects related to RF emissions," Wessel said. He stated that the BioInitiative Report seems to completely dismiss the Nationwide Cohort Study in Denmark by Christoffer Johansen, John D. Boice Jr., Joseph K. McLaughlin and Jorgen H. Olsen, which included 420,095 cell phone users and found no significant link between cell phone use and cancer.

Wessel called it peculiar that the BioInitiative Report suggests RF exposure limits be reduced to increase the safety margin against the possibility of nonthermal effects on humans without offering specifics on what those limits should be, beyond the suggestion that "a precautionary limit of 0.1 µW/cm2 (which is also 0.614 volts per meter) should be adopted for outdoor, cumulative RF exposure." The irony, Wessel explained, is that any properly designed cellular and PCS site, which would have antennas at least 10 meters above ground level, already contributes less than what the BioInitiative Report proposes as a precautionary limit to areas surrounding those sites. He pointed out that commercial TV and FM broadcast levels typically exceed this precautionary limit in every major metropolitan location in the country: "Curiously, they choose to ignore an RF source that has been present for several decades."

**"Better science."** Wessel said that although the BioInitiative Report appears to have as its objective making the case for eliminating or reducing wireless communications, in several places the report admits there is no definitive link between cell phones and cancer. In preparing his presentation, Wessel viewed a website built by one of those opposed to the tower: "He had the BioInitiative Report on his site along with other information depicting a one-sided view against cell towers."

**Measurement equipment.** Wessel presented the board a different perspective based on quantitative RF measurements taken with a selective radiation meter, which consists of a spectrum analyzer and an isotropic antenna — the Narda SRM-3000. He said this meter is one of a few portable spectrum analyzers designed and calibrated specifically to make safety measurements for RF compliance and to provide evidence that energy levels may be many times less than the safety minimum. "It has a dynamic range much greater than broadband equipment specifically designed to perform RF compliance measurements," he said, adding that "you can discriminate these measurements by frequency from 50 to 3000 MHz. This enables us to specifically measure each license holder's contribution to the overall RF environment."

**The handset exposure argument.** Wessel described the RF measurement data that was persuasive for the Marshalltown board. "They were concerned about the RF level that would be present at the high school if they allowed the cell site to be built. Actually, the larger risk of RF exposure comes from the cellular handset itself, even though it's still greatly below the FCC limits." He cited the inverse-square law, which says that the RF energy at a distance from a source drops by the square of the distance from the source.

At the Marshalltown school, cellular service is provided by sites a mile or two away, which causes the handsets used at the school to emit their highest RF power output, because the distant cell site controls handset power and raises or lowers it according to the received signal (uplink) at the cell site. "I took measurements at the school, and they indicated the handsets were powered up to full power during a call because of the distance to the serving cell site," Wessel said. "I told the board that it could reduce the RF exposure to students using phones by putting a site nearby because then the handsets would operate at significantly lower power. If you have a quarter-watt handset next to your head, it delivers significantly more energy to the user than does a 100-watt cell site 100 feet away and 100 feet above the ground, because of the inverse-square law."

"But no one ever looks at it that way," Wessel said. "They see the cell site as an RF radiation problem next to the school. But ironically, when you put the cell site next to a high school, where kids are huge users of handsets, the handset's power is significantly reduced by thousands of times. A nearby site actually helps the issue." One parent observed that students have handsets near their heads all the time. "Our measurements proved that with a nearby cell site, RF exposure from the handsets would be reduced from a level 1,000 times (peak) below the FCC-defined safety limit to a level 1 million times below the safety limit," Wessel said. "A majority of the board members were persuaded by this approach. But some people are never satisfied."

**Actual measurements and public reaction.** Wessel said the fact is that handsets are going to be powered down if the cell site is nearby, and the RF exposure from the handset is the greater risk. Despite the evidence, some people do not want to look at the actual measurements, and their objection is sometimes based on hysteria. "The cell sites look ominous, but the power reaching the ground in the vicinity of the site is insignificant," he said. He also described measurements he made in a New York City neighborhood where RF energy reaching the neighborhood from FM and TV broadcast signals is a greater percentage of the overall RF energy than the portion delivered by a cell site across the street. "They don't want to hear that, either," he said of residents opposing a neighborhood cell site. "They fear the long-term effects of RF exposure from cell sites, yet FM and TV signals have been on the air for a lot longer than cellular signals, they represent a higher percentage of the overall RF exposure than the cellular signals do, and the total is still well below the safety limit."

**Common-sense approach and narrowband selectivity.** Wessel said the idea is to present information in a common-sense approach. "You're never going to change the opinion of a skeptic or of the conspiracy theorists who want to believe that the explosion in cell site growth will cause significant health risks," he said. "They call it new technology, but it's merely a new application of old technology. You can rarely change their minds. You try to present a common-sense approach to people who have become emotional by the surrounding hysteria. The cellular site opponents get people worked up and cite possible children's health effects in an effort to convince them that the cellular sites are harming the kids." With measurement equipment capable of narrowband selectivity, Wessel said, it is possible to select a frequency and measure power density levels down to the picowatt per square centimeter level: "It allows you to demonstrate that cell sites are not a big deal."

**Illustrations.** Photographs show Wessel using a selective radiation meter to take measurements and taking RF measurements near a cellular antenna disguised as a saguaro cactus; the captions note that a person would have to scale the cactus to the antennas hidden near its top to receive unsafe RF exposure, and that although a worker on a tower may come close enough to an antenna — especially FM or TV broadcast antennas — to require protection in the form of an RF suit, the inverse-square law shows the intensity of RF from an antenna rapidly diminishes as distance increases, so that away from the tower energy levels rarely surpass the health limit, especially for cellular antennas.
